title: Give OutboxProcessor's single-flight guard a generation token so stale-reclaim can't run concurrent drains

evidence.quote: // reclaim only inspects the *same instance's* private state we also

why: The single-flight guard is two plain fields (_draining/_drainingSince) with no per-invocation identity. In production, OutboxProcessor is built with unmodified defaults (outbox_providers.dart:98-105: pushTimeout/drainStaleAfter never overridden) and sync_orchestrator.dart fires a periodic drain every 60s forever (Timer.periodic(_periodicDrainInterval, ...)) while drainStaleAfter is 90s. Non-completion kinds are pushed one row at a time, individually awaited (up to 50 rows x ~18 kinds) — a real multi-kind backlog on a slow connection easily exceeds 90s. When that happens, the next periodic (or connectivity/lifecycle) trigger sees the guard as 'stale', resets it, and starts a second, genuinely concurrent `_doDrain()` while the first is still running — the code comment at line 206-211 only reasons about two *reclaimers* racing each other synchronously; it never accounts for the *original* stale-but-still-running drain's own `finally` unconditionally zeroing `_draining`/`_drainingSince` once it eventually completes, which can then let a THIRD trigger barge in on top of the second. This directly breaks the documented contract ('collapses them to one push round' / sync_orchestrator.dart:568 'the OutboxProcessor's single-flight guard collapses races with other triggers'), producing duplicate concurrent Firestore pushes and racy interleaved deleteRow/markAttempted calls that can double-count a row's attempts and dead-letter a recoverable failure roughly twice as fast as _maxAttempts=10 implies. The R6-13 regression test that targets exactly this code path never builds true overlap: every scenario releases and awaits the 'wedged' pipeline to full completion before the next drain runs (its own comment admits the limitation at line 1392/1396), so the actual race is untested.
recommendation: Replace the boolean+timestamp guard with a construct that can tell 'my invocation' apart from a later reclaimer — e.g. a monotonically increasing generation counter captured at acquire time, checked before `finally` clears state (`if (_generation == myGeneration) { _draining = false; ... }`), or switch to chaining onto the in-flight Future (a late caller awaits/joins the existing drain rather than racing a flag).
acceptance_criteria: New/updated unit test keeps the first drain's pipeline call parked on a Completer, advances the clock past drainStaleAfter, drives a second (reclaiming) drain to full completion, then completes the first — and asserts the pipeline was invoked exactly once for the outstanding rows, or that DAO state is never corrupted by true overlap.
Guard implementation carries a generation token (or equivalent) so a finally block from an earlier invocation cannot clear state established by a later one.

corrections: The finding's characterization of the R6-13 test as "never builds true overlap" is only partially accurate. Two of its three sub-scenarios (p and p2) do complete the wedged drain before proceeding. But the third sub-scenario (p3, using _TogglePipeline, lines 1440-1483) genuinely does produce true overlap: setting `hang=false` does not unblock the already-parked first call (only affects future calls), so `reclaimedCount = await p3.drain(profileId)` at line 1464 runs concurrently with the still-suspended wedgedDrain3. However, the test asserts nothing about the consequence of that overlap (no pipeline-invocation-count or DAO-corruption assertion, just `>=1`), so the finding's substantive point — no regression test guards against duplicate/racy work from true overlap — still holds even though the "never builds true overlap" phrasing overstates the test's limitation.
